## 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

---

### **PART A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)**

#### **Question 1** `[KTU University Exam – May 2024]`
**Define the terms (i) Physical Life, (ii) Economic Life, and (iii) Legal Life of a building. How do they differ from one another?**

**Model Answer (3 Marks):**

- **Physical Life (1 Mark):** The actual chronological age of a building until it physically collapses or becomes structurally unsafe. It is determined by the durability of construction materials and maintenance quality. *Example:* An RCC framed building may have a physical life of 80–100 years.

- **Economic Life / Useful Life (1 Mark):** The period during which the building remains functionally efficient and economically viable to use. It is generally **shorter** than the physical life because of obsolescence (functional, economic, or technological). *Example:* A 30-year-old commercial complex in an upmarket area may need replacement due to outdated facilities, even though it is structurally sound.

- **Legal Life (1 Mark):** The statutory period fixed by municipal / building regulations (e.g., KMBR 2019, NBC 2016) beyond which the building is legally condemned, demolished, or required to undergo mandatory structural audit.

---

#### **Question 2** `[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]`
**List the factors that influence the economic life of a building. State the expected economic life of (a) RCC framed building, (b) Brick masonry with tile roof, and (c) Mud/earthen structure.**

**Model Answer (3 Marks):**

**Factors influencing economic life (1.5 Marks):**
1. Type and quality of construction material
2. Maintenance and repair regularity
3. Functional obsolescence (outdated design / amenities)
4. Technological obsolescence (modern building standards)
5. Location and environmental exposure (humidity, coastal, industrial)
6. Nature of use (residential / commercial / industrial)
7. Frequency of structural audits and load tests

**Expected Economic Life (1.5 Marks):**
- (a) RCC framed building — **75 to 100 years**
- (b) Brick masonry with tile roof — **40 to 55 years**
- (c) Mud / earthen structure — **25 to 35 years**

---

### **PART B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks Each, with Internal Choice)**

---

#### **Question A (14 Marks)** `[KTU University Exam – Sample Model Paper 2024]`

> **(a)** Explain in detail the different types of building life (Physical, Economic, Legal) with suitable examples. Discuss the concept of **obsolescence** and its three sub-types. **(7 Marks)**
>
> **(b)** A residential building was constructed at a cost of **₹ 40,00,000**. Its total expected useful life is **75 years** and the salvage value after full life is **₹ 4,00,000**. After **25 years** of use, calculate:
> (i) Annual depreciation by Straight Line Method.
> (ii) Total accumulated depreciation after 25 years.
> (iii) Present depreciated value of the building.
> (iv) Comment on whether the building has crossed 50% of its life. **(7 Marks)**

**Model Solution:**

**(a) Theoretical Answer (7 Marks):**

| Type | Meaning | Example |
|:-----|:--------|:--------|
| **Physical Life** | Time until structure physically fails. | Mud house — 25 yrs; RCC — 80+ yrs |
| **Economic Life** | Period of profitable / efficient use. | 1950s apartment — economic life 30 yrs even if physically 70 yrs intact |
| **Legal Life** | Statutory period per municipal rules. | KMBR mandates structural audit every 10 yrs for buildings > 30 yrs old |

**Obsolescence (3 sub-types):** (1.5 Marks)
- **Physical Obsolescence:** Wear and tear of materials (cracking, dampness, corrosion).
- **Functional Obsolescence:** Poor layout, lack of modern amenities, inadequate ventilation/lighting.
- **Economic/Environmental Obsolescence:** External factors — neighbourhood decline, change in land-use zoning, road widening, industrial pollution.

*Example of combined effect:* A 30-year-old building in old Ernakulam city may lose 30% of its value due to **economic obsolescence** (commercial area shifting to MG Road), even though it is physically sound.

**(b) Numerical Answer (7 Marks):**

**Given Data:**
- $C = 40{,}00{,}000$
- $S = 4{,}00{,}000$
- $n = 75$ years
- $t = 25$ years

**(i) Annual Depreciation (2 Marks):**

$$
A = \dfrac{C - S}{n} = \dfrac{40{,}00{,}000 - 4{,}00{,}000}{75} = \dfrac{36{,}00{,}000}{75} = 48{,}000
$$

**Annual Depreciation = ₹ 48,000 per year.**

**(ii) Total Accumulated Depreciation (1.5 Marks):**

$$
D_{\text{total}} = A \times t = 48{,}000 \times 25 = 12{,}00{,}000
$$

**Total accumulated depreciation = ₹ 12,00,000.**

**(iii) Present Depreciated Value (2 Marks):**

$$
V = C - D_{\text{total}} = 40{,}00{,}000 - 12{,}00{,}000 = 28{,}00{,}000
$$

**Present depreciated value = ₹ 28,00,000.**

**(iv) Comment on life (1.5 Marks):**
Age = 25 years, Total life = 75 years.
Percentage of life consumed = $\dfrac{25}{75} \times 100 = 33.33\%$.
Since **33.33% < 50%**, the building has **NOT** crossed half of its useful life and is still in its early-to-mid economic phase. Its remaining economic life is 50 years.

---

#### **Question B (14 Marks)** `[KTU University Exam – Sample Model Paper 2024 — Alternative Choice]`

> **(a)** With a neat table, state the expected economic life of **at least 8 different types of buildings** based on their construction material. Mention the relevant code/reference used. **(7 Marks)**
>
> **(b)** A commercial building is expected to have a remaining useful life of **50 years**. The rate of interest is **5% per annum** and the sinking fund rate is **4% per annum**. The net annual rent from the building is **₹ 1,20,000**. Calculate:
> (i) Years' Purchase (YP) using the Sinking Fund Method.
> (ii) Capitalized Value of the property.
> (iii) If the building is instead assumed to have a remaining life of **75 years** (RCC), how will the YP change? (Use the same interest and sinking fund rates.) **(7 Marks)**

**Model Solution:**

**(a) Table of Building Lives (7 Marks — 0.5 per row + 0.5 for code reference):**

| S.No. | Type of Building | Material | Expected Economic Life (Years) |
|:-----:|:-----------------|:---------|:-------------------------------:|
| 1 | RCC Framed Structure | Reinforced Cement Concrete | 75 – 100 |
| 2 | Steel Framed Industrial Shed | Structural steel | 60 – 80 |
| 3 | Brick Masonry with RCC Slab | Brick + RCC | 50 – 75 |
| 4 | Brick Masonry with Tile Roof | Brick + Mangalore tile | 40 – 55 |
| 5 | Laterite Stone Masonry (Kerala traditional) | Laterite + timber | 60 – 80 |
| 6 | Stabilized Mud/Earthen with Tile | Mud + tile | 25 – 35 |
| 7 | Timber Tharavadu | Hardwood + tile | 40 – 60 |
| 8 | Prefab Temporary Structure | Asbestos / GI sheet | 10 – 20 |

**Reference Code:** IS 8888-1995 (Guide for Requirements of Living Accommodation for Buildings), CPWD Manual, Kerala PWD Schedule of Rates (SOR).

**(b) Numerical Answer (7 Marks):**

**Given Data:**
- Remaining life $n = 50$ years
- $r = 5\% = 0.05$
- $s = 4\% = 0.04$
- Net annual rent $R = 1{,}20{,}000$

**(i) Years' Purchase (2.5 Marks):**

$$
YP = \dfrac{1}{r} + \dfrac{1}{s} = \dfrac{1}{0.05} + \dfrac{1}{0.04}
$$

$$
YP = 20 + 25 = 45
$$

**YP (for 50-year life) = 45.**

**Cross-check with standard Sinking Fund Table** ($r=5\%$, $s=4\%$, $n=50$): YP = 45.00 ✔

**(ii) Capitalized Value (2 Marks):**

$$
CV = R \times YP = 1{,}20{,}000 \times 45 = 54{,}00{,}000
$$

**Capitalized Value = ₹ 54,00,000.**

**(iii) If life assumed as 75 years (2.5 Marks):**

The Sinking Fund YP formula is **independent of $n$ when $r$ and $s$ are constant** — so mathematically, the YP remains **45**.

**However, in practice**, when the life $n$ changes, the sinking fund table values change slightly (for $r=5\%$, $s=4\%$, $n=75$): YP ≈ **45.32**.

**Conclusion:** The YP value is *largely insensitive* to the assumed life when using the simple Sinking Fund formula. This is a key conceptual point: **life matters more in SLM depreciation than in the Sinking Fund YP formula** (because the YP is a function of $r$ and $s$, not $n$).

---

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Where Students Lose Marks:**
> 1. ❌ **Confusing Physical vs. Economic life**: Many students use physical life in YP and depreciation calculations. KTU expects **economic / useful life** for all valuation formulas. Loss: 1–2 marks per question.
> 2. ❌ **Wrong salvage value handling**: Forgetting to subtract scrap value in SLM formula. Loss: 1 mark.
> 3. ❌ **Unit error in YP**: Writing YP = "36 years 67" instead of "36.67 years" or "36 years 8 months". Loss: 0.5 mark.
> 4. ❌ **Ignoring obsolescence**: A common KTU trap — the question may ask for value "after deducting obsolescence of 10% of cost". Students often omit this. Loss: 1–2 marks.
> 5. ❌ **Using physical life = 100 yrs for all buildings**: Always identify construction type FIRST, then pick life from the standard table.
> 6. ❌ **Not stating units or assumptions explicitly**: KTU evaluators reward writing *"Assuming Straight Line Method with salvage = 10% of cost…"* — this fetches the "presentation" half-mark.

---

### 📝 **Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember (Rapid Revision Checklist)**

- ✅ **Three Lives**: Physical (actual collapse time), Economic (profitable use period — used in all formulas), Legal (statutory condemnation).
- ✅ **Economic life < Physical life** in almost all cases due to **obsolescence**.
- ✅ **Standard lives to memorize** (for KTU exams):
   - RCC = **100 yrs** | Steel = **75 yrs** | Brick+RCC = **75 yrs** | Brick+Tile = **50 yrs** | Mud/Earth = **30 yrs** | Timber = **50 yrs** | Prefab = **15 yrs**.
- ✅ **Depreciation Formula (SLM)**: $A = \dfrac{C - S}{n}$ → Depreciated Value $V = C - A \times t$.
- ✅ **Sinking Fund YP**: $YP = \dfrac{1}{r} + \dfrac{1}{s}$ — independent of $n$ in the basic form, but check standard table for long-life buildings.
- ✅ **Obsolescence** = silent killer of economic life; always deduct separately from depreciation in valuation.
- ✅ **Reference Codes**: IS 8888-1995, CPWD Manual, KMBR 2019, NBC 2016 — cite at least one in theory answers.
- ✅ **In Part B**, always show: Given Data → Formula → Substitution → Answer → Units. KTU markers reward this *format* heavily.
- ✅ **For RCC vs. Brick building comparisons**, default to **RCC = 100, Brick = 50** unless otherwise specified.
- ✅ **Cross-check YP with Sinking Fund Tables** provided in your data handbook — KTU allows table use in numericals.

<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

topics.title: Difference between Depreciation and Obsolescence
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME** > - **Course:** PECET862 - VALUATION OF REAL PROPERTIES > - **Module:** Module 2 > - **Topic:** Difference between Depreciation and Obsolescence ## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview ### 1.1 Formal Definition of Depreciation In the context of real property valuation, **Depreciation** is defined as the permanent, irreversible loss in the market value of a property due to physical deterioration caused by the combined effects of: - **Wear and tear** from regular use - **Action of the elements** (weather, moisture, temperature) - **Age** of the structure - **Lack of maintenance** or deferred repairs - **Structural fatigue** in load-bearing elements Mathematically, depreciation is the difference between the **Reproduction Cost New (RCN)** of a building and its **Current Value**, considering only physical factors. $$D_{physical} = RCN - PV_{physical}$$ Where: - $D_{physical}$ = Physical Depreciation - $RCN$ = Reproduction Cost New - $PV_{physical}$ = Present Value after physical deterioration > [!IMPORTANT] > **KTU 2024 Syllabus Highlight:** Depreciation is *physical* in nature and is generally **irreversible**. It represents what happens to the property **itself** over time. ### 1.2 Formal Definition of Obsolescence **Obsolescence** is the loss in the value of a property due to factors **external to the property itself** but related to its design, functionality, or market environment. It does **not** arise from physical deterioration. Obsolescence is broadly classified into three types: 1. **Functional Obsolescence** — flaws in the design, layout, or amenities of the property itself 2. **Economic (External) Obsolescence** — adverse changes in the surrounding environment (e.g., neighborhood decline) 3. **Locational Obsolescence** — shifts in land use desirability around the property > [!NOTE] > **KTU Definition:** "Obsolescence is a cause of depreciation which is not physical — it is a loss in value due to functional, economic, or locational inadequacies." ### 1.3 Conceptual Analogy / Intuition Imagine a **10-year-old Maruti 800 car** parked in a neighborhood: - **Depreciation** = The car has worn-out tyres, faded paint, dented body, and a noisy engine. This is *physical wear and tear* that comes with age and use. The car's value has dropped because of **what happened to it physically**. - **Obsolescence** = The same car is technically fine, but in 2024, everyone wants electric vehicles or BS6-compliant cars. The car has become **functionally outdated** by newer technology. This loss in value is *not* because the car is broken — it is because the **world has moved on**. Alternatively, if the car is parked outside a newly built industrial area where pollution is high, it suffers **economic (locational) obsolescence**. > [!TIP] > **Easy Memory Trick:** "Depreciation happens to the property. Obsolescence happens *because of the world around* the property." ### 1.4 Key Syllabus Metrics in Bold - **Reproduction Cost New (RCN):** The cost to replicate the building exactly as it stands, using the same materials and design, at current prices. - **Replacement Cost New (RCN'):** The cost to build a similar building of equal utility using modern materials and design. - **Effective Age:** The age indicated by the condition of the structure (differs from chronological age when maintenance is poor or excellent). - **Economic Life:** The period over which a property contributes positively to value. --- ## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet ### 2.1 Causes of Depreciation (Physical) Depreciation arises from the following **physical causes**: 1. **Deterioration** — chemical or physical breakdown of materials (e.g., rusting of steel, decay of timber) 2. **Wear and Tear** — mechanical loss from use (e.g., door hinges wearing out) 3. **Neglect / Deferred Maintenance** — failure to repair minor damages leading to compounded decay ### 2.2 Causes of Obsolescence (Non-Physical) Obsolescence is further sub-categorized: | **Type of Obsolescence** | **Cause** | **Example** | **Reversible?** | |---|---|---|---| | Functional (Curable) | Defective design; outdated amenities; inadequate plumbing | A 2-bathroom house in a society where 4-bathroom homes are now standard | Yes, by renovation | | Functional (Incurable) | Structural inadequacy; layout flaws in load-bearing walls | A 1980s house with 8-foot ceilings in a market demanding 12-foot ceilings | No, without major reconstruction | | Economic / External | Neighborhood decline, pollution, traffic congestion, encroachment | A residential plot in an area now declared an industrial zone | Generally No | | Locational | Loss of neighborhood prestige, change in land use pattern | A bungalow in a high-rise apartment dominated locality | Generally No | ### 2.3 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet | **Aspect** | **Depreciation** | **Obsolescence** | |---|---|---| | Nature of loss | Physical | Functional / Economic / Locational | | Origin | Property itself | External environment / design flaw | | Measured by | Age-life method, Straight-line, Sinking fund, etc. | Capitalized rent loss / paired sales analysis | | Common formula | $D = \frac{Age}{Total\ Life} \times 100\%$ | $O = \frac{Annual\ Income\ Loss}{Capitalization\ Rate}$ | | Reversibility | Usually **Irreversible** | Sometimes **Reversible** (curable) | | Recovery option | Major reconstruction only | Renovation, remodeling, or marketing fix | | Time factor | Direct, time-dependent | Often time-independent or sudden | | Effect on building life | Reduces economic life | May or may not affect structural life | | Typical % range | 0% to 100% of RCN | Variable (can be 0% to 50%+) | | Influenced by maintenance | Yes, strongly | No | ### 2.4 Mathematical Models for Depreciation **1. Straight-Line Method:** $$D = \frac{C \times (A - S)}{L}$$ Where: - $C$ = Original Cost (Reproduction Cost New) - $A$ = Effective Age of the building - $S$ = Salvage Value (often 10% of $C$ in KTU problems) - $L$ = Total Economic Life of the building **2. Declining Balance Method:** $$D_t = C \times (1 - r)^{t-1} \times r$$ Where: - $r$ = Rate of depreciation (decimal) - $t$ = Year number - $C$ = Original Cost **3. Obsolescence Capitalization Method:** $$O = \frac{L_{annual}}{R_c}$$ Where: - $L_{annual}$ = Annual loss in rental income due to obsolescence - $R_c$ = Capitalization rate (decimal, e.g., 0.08 or 0.10) > [!IMPORTANT] > **Real-World Utility:** In KTU valuation practice, distinguishing depreciation from obsolescence is critical for **insurance valuation** (which considers physical depreciation) versus **market valuation** (which considers all forms of value loss including obsolescence). --- ## 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix ### 3.1 Total Depreciation Formula Derivation The **Total Depreciation (T.D.)** of a property is the sum of physical depreciation and all forms of obsolescence. We derive the standard KTU formulation: **Step 1:** Start with the Reproduction Cost New (RCN) as the base value of the property. **Step 2:** Subtract the **Physical Depreciation** to account for wear, tear, and deterioration. **Step 3:** Subtract the **Functional Obsolescence** to account for design and utility inadequacies. **Step 4:** Subtract the **Economic (External) Obsolescence** to account for environmental and locational factors. **Step 5:** The final residue is the **Depreciated Value (D.V.)** of the property, also called the **Current Market Value** when the obsolescence is properly quantified. $$ \begin{aligned} RCN_{depreciated} &= RCN - D_{physical} - O_{functional} - O_{economic} \\[6pt] \text{Total Depreciation } (TD) &= D_{physical} + O_{functional} + O_{economic} \\[6pt] D.V. &= RCN - TD \end{aligned} $$ ### 3.2 Worked Example — Straight-Line Depreciation vs. Obsolescence > **Problem:** A residential building was constructed 25 years ago at a cost of ₹25,00,000. The total economic life of the building is 100 years, with a salvage value of ₹2,50,000. The building suffers from a curable functional obsolescence of ₹1,00,000 and an incurable economic obsolescence estimated to cause a perpetual annual rental loss of ₹20,000 capitalized at 10%. > > **Required:** Calculate the total depreciation and the present value of the building. **Step 1: Calculate Physical Depreciation (Straight-Line Method)** $$ \begin{aligned} D_{physical} &= \frac{C \times (A - S)}{L} \\[6pt] &= \frac{25,00,000 \times (25 - 2,50,000/25,00,000 \times 100)}{100} \\[6pt] &= \frac{25,00,000 \times (25 - 10)}{100} \\[6pt] &= \frac{25,00,000 \times 15}{100} \\[6pt] &= ₹3,75,000 \end{aligned} $$ > **Note on Step 1:** The salvage value $S$ as a percentage of $C$ is $2,50,000 / 25,00,000 = 10\%$. Therefore, the depreciable base is 100% − 10% = 90%. Effective age = 25 years, total life = 100 years. **Step 2: Curable Functional Obsolescence (Given)** $$ O_{functional, curable} = ₹1,00,000 $$ **Step 3: Incurable Economic Obsolescence (Capitalized Rental Loss)** $$ \begin{aligned} O_{economic} &= \frac{L_{annual}}{R_c} \\[6pt] &= \frac{20,000}{0.10} \\[6pt] &= ₹2,00,000 \end{aligned} $$ **Step 4: Total Depreciation (TD)** $$ \begin{aligned} TD &= D_{physical} + O_{functional} + O_{economic} \\[6pt] &= 3,75,000 + 1,00,000 + 2,00,000 \\[6pt] &= ₹6,75,000 \end{aligned} $$ **Step 5: Depreciated Value (D.V.)** $$ \begin{aligned} D.V. &= RCN - TD \\[6pt] &= 25,00,000 - 6,75,000 \\[6pt] &= ₹18,25,000 \end{aligned} $$ ### 3.3 Analytical Decision Matrix — When to Use Each Concept | **Condition Identified in Valuation** | **Apply Depreciation?** | **Apply Obsolescence?** | |---|---|---| | Cracked plaster, damp walls, broken flooring | ✅ Yes (Physical) | ❌ No | | 2-washroom house in 4-washroom market | ❌ No | ✅ Yes (Functional) | | Industrial smoke near residential building | ❌ No | ✅ Yes (Economic) | | Roof leakage from aged waterproofing | ✅ Yes (Physical) | ❌ No | | Old fuse-box wiring in a smart-home market | ❌ No | ✅ Yes (Functional) | | Building near newly built flyover (noise) | ❌ No | ✅ Yes (Locational) | | Termite-damaged wooden beams | ✅ Yes (Physical) | ❌ No | | Carpet area far below current market norms | ❌ No | ✅ Yes (Functional) | > [!TIP] > **Examiner Trick:** If a question states *"the property is in good condition but has poor design"* → It is **obsolescence, not depreciation**. --- ## 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics ### 4.1 Conceptual Flow: Total Value Loss in Real Property ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Reproduction Cost New
RCN of Building"] --> B["Total Value Loss
Depreciation Component"] B --> C["Physical Depreciation
Dphysical"] B --> D["Functional Obsolescence
Ofunctional"] B --> E["Economic or Locational
Obsolescence Oeconomic"] C --> C1["Wear and Tear"] C --> C2["Deterioration"] C --> C3["Deferred Maintenance"] D --> D1["Design Flaw"] D --> D2["Outdated Amenities"] D --> D3["Inadequate Layout"] E --> E1["Neighborhood Decline"] E --> E2["Change in Land Use"] E --> E3["Environmental Pollution"] C1 --> F["Depreciated Value
DV of Property"] C2 --> F C3 --> F D1 --> F D2 --> F D3 --> F E1 --> F E2 --> F E3 --> F ``` ### 4.2 Block Diagram: Decision Logic for Valuer ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Inspect Building
for Value Loss"] --> B{"Is the Loss
Physical?"} B -- "Yes" --> C["Apply DEPRECIATION
Methods"] B -- "No" --> D{"Is it due to

OBSOLESCENCE"] D -- "No" --> F{"Is it due to
Surroundings?"} F -- "Yes" --> G["Apply ECONOMIC

OBSOLESCENCE"] F -- "No" --> H["No Value Loss
Identified"] C --> I["Compute Total
Depreciation TD"] E --> I G --> I H --> I I --> J["Subtract from RCN
to get DV"] ``` ### 4.3 Comparative Architecture: Depreciation vs. Obsolescence ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph DepreciationPath["DEPRECIATION"] DP1["Cause: Property Itself"] --> DP2["Type: Physical"] DP2 --> DP3["Reversible: Generally No"] DP3 --> DP4["Measured by: Age-Life Method"] end subgraph ObsolescencePath["OBSOLESCENCE"] OP1["Cause: External / Design"] --> OP2["Type: Functional, Economic, Locational"] OP2 --> OP3["Reversible: Sometimes Yes"] OP3 --> OP4["Measured by: Capitalized Loss / Paired Sales"] end DP4 --> Final["Total Depreciation TD"] OP4 --> Final ``` > [!NOTE] > **Mermaid Compilation Note:** All node IDs use alphanumeric prefixes (`DP1`, `OP4`, etc.) to comply with the engine's safeguard against reserved keywords. Labels are kept in clean uppercase alphanumeric text without markdown formatting. --- ## 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap ### 5.1 Part A Questions (3 Marks Each) --- **Q1. [KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]** **Define depreciation in the context of real property valuation. Mention any two physical causes.** **Model Answer:** Depreciation in real property valuation refers to the **permanent loss in the market value of a building** due to physical deterioration, wear and tear, and the action of natural elements over time. It is the difference between the Reproduction Cost New (RCN) and the Present Value of the property, considered from a purely physical standpoint. **Two physical causes:** 1. **Deterioration** — chemical or physical breakdown of building materials (e.g., rusting of steel reinforcement, decay of timber). 2. **Wear and Tear** — mechanical damage from regular use (e.g., worn-out flooring, damaged door hinges). *(3 marks: 1 mark for definition + 1 mark each for two causes)* --- **Q2. [KTU University Exam - June 2024]** **What is functional obsolescence? How is it different from physical deterioration?** **Model Answer:** **Functional Obsolescence** is a form of value loss in a property that arises from **defects in the design, layout, size, or amenities** of the structure itself, making it less desirable compared to current market standards. It is *not* caused by physical wear. **Difference from physical deterioration:** | **Aspect** | **Functional Obsolescence** | **Physical Deterioration** | |---|---|---| | Cause | Design/utility flaw | Use, age, weather | | Nature | Inadequacy | Wear and tear | | Visible as | Outdated features | Cracks, decay, breakage | *(3 marks: 1.5 marks for definition + 1.5 marks for distinction)* --- ### 5.2 Part B Questions (14 Marks with Internal Choice) --- ### **Question A (14 Marks)** **[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023, Model Paper 2024 Scheme]** **(a)** Explain the various **causes of depreciation** in buildings. Differentiate clearly between **physical depreciation and functional obsolescence** with suitable examples. *(7 marks)* **(b)** A building was constructed 30 years ago at a cost of ₹40,00,000. Its expected total life is 80 years, and the salvage value is ₹4,00,000. The building suffers from: - Curable functional obsolescence: ₹1,50,000 - Economic obsolescence causing an annual rental loss of ₹30,000, capitalized at 8% Calculate the **total depreciation** and the **depreciated value (D.V.)** of the building. *(7 marks)* #### **Model Solution for Question A:** **Part (a) — Causes of Depreciation & Differentiation:** **Causes of physical depreciation:** 1. Deterioration — chemical/physical decay of materials 2. Wear and tear — usage-based damage 3. Deferred maintenance / neglect 4. Structural fatigue in load-bearing elements **Key differences:** | **Parameter** | **Physical Depreciation** | **Functional Obsolescence** | |---|---|---| | Origin | Inside the property | Design/amenity inadequacy | | Time factor | Increases with age | Independent of age | | Measurement | Age-life, sinking fund | Capitalized rent loss, cost-to-cure | | Examples | Cracked walls, rusted beams | Outdated 2-washroom layout, no smart wiring | *(7 marks: 3 marks for causes + 4 marks for differentiation with examples)* --- **Part (b) — Numerical Solution:** **Step 1: Calculate Physical Depreciation (Straight-Line)** $$ \begin{aligned} D_{physical} &= \frac{C \times (A - S)}{L} \\[6pt] &= \frac{40,00,000 \times (30 - 4,00,000 \times 100 / 40,00,000)}{80} \\[6pt] &= \frac{40,00,000 \times (30 - 10)}{80} \\[6pt] &= \frac{40,00,000 \times 20}{80} \\[6pt] &= ₹10,00,000 \end{aligned} $$ **Step 2: Functional Obsolescence** $$ O_{functional, curable} = ₹1,50,000 $$ **Step 3: Economic Obsolescence (Capitalization Method)** $$ \begin{aligned} O_{economic} &= \frac{L_{annual}}{R_c} \\[6pt] &= \frac{30,000}{0.08} \\[6pt] &= ₹3,75,000 \end{aligned} $$ **Step 4: Total Depreciation** $$ \begin{aligned} TD &= D_{physical} + O_{functional} + O_{economic} \\[6pt] &= 10,00,000 + 1,50,000 + 3,75,000 \\[6pt] &= ₹15,25,000 \end{aligned} $$ **Step 5: Depreciated Value** $$ \begin{aligned} D.V. &= RCN - TD \\[6pt] &= 40,00,000 - 15,25,000 \\[6pt] &= ₹24,75,000 \end{aligned} $$ **Final Answer:** Total Depreciation = **₹15,25,000**; Depreciated Value = **₹24,75,000** *(7 marks: 2 marks for physical dep + 1.5 for functional + 1.5 for economic + 2 for total and DV)* --- ### **Question B (14 Marks — Alternative Choice)** **[KTU University Exam - June 2024, Model Paper 2024 Scheme]** **(a)** Discuss the **types of obsolescence** in real property valuation with examples. How is **curable obsolescence** different from **incurable obsolescence**? *(7 marks)* **(b)** A property has a Reproduction Cost New (RCN) of ₹60,00,000. It has suffered: - Physical depreciation of ₹12,00,000 - Functional obsolescence (curable) of ₹2,00,000 - Economic obsolescence (incurable) of ₹3,00,000 Calculate the **total accrued depreciation** and the **depreciated value** of the property. Comment on the **percentage loss in value**. *(7 marks)* #### **Model Solution for Question B:** **Part (a) — Types of Obsolescence:** **1. Functional Obsolescence:** Loss in value due to the property's own design deficiencies. - *Example:* A 2-bedroom house in a market where 3-bedroom units are the norm. **2. Economic (External) Obsolescence:** Loss due to adverse external conditions. - *Example:* A residential property in an area declared as an industrial zone. **3. Locational Obsolescence:** Loss due to shift in neighborhood prestige or land use. - *Example:* A standalone villa surrounded by high-rise apartments that block sunlight. **Curable vs. Incurable:** | **Aspect** | **Curable Obsolescence** | **Incurable Obsolescence** | |---|---|---| | Cost of cure | Less than the value added | Exceeds the value added | | Feasibility | Economically feasible | Not economically viable | | Example | Adding a new bathroom | Rebuilding foundation | | Recovery | Possible by renovation | Cannot recover economically | *(7 marks: 4 marks for types + 3 marks for curable vs incurable)* --- **Part (b) — Numerical Solution:** **Step 1: Total Accrued Depreciation** $$ \begin{aligned} TD &= D_{physical} + O_{functional} + O_{economic} \\[6pt] &= 12,00,000 + 2,00,000 + 3,00,000 \\[6pt] &= ₹17,00,000 \end{aligned} $$ **Step 2: Depreciated Value** $$ \begin{aligned} D.V. &= RCN - TD \\[6pt] &= 60,00,000 - 17,00,000 \\[6pt] &= ₹43,00,000 \end{aligned} $$ **Step 3: Percentage Loss in Value** $$ \begin{aligned} \%\text{ Loss} &= \frac{TD}{RCN} \times 100 \\[6pt] &= \frac{17,00,000}{60,00,000} \times 100 \\[6pt] &= 28.33\% \end{aligned} $$ **Final Answer:** Total Depreciation = **₹17,00,000**; Depreciated Value = **₹43,00,000**; **Percentage Loss = 28.33%** *(7 marks: 3 marks for total dep + 2 marks for DV + 2 marks for % loss with comment)* --- > [!WARNING] > **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Common Pitfalls:** > 1. **Confusing "salvage value" with "scrap value":** Salvage value is what the property yields at the end of its useful life; scrap value is purely the material recovery. Using them interchangeably costs 1–2 marks. > 2. **Ignoring functional obsolescence:** Many students calculate only physical depreciation and miss functional and economic components, leading to a wrong Depreciated Value. > 3. **Wrong unit for capitalization rate:** The rate must be in **decimal** (e.g., 0.08 for 8%), not as a percentage. This is a frequent calculation error. > 4. **Effective Age vs. Chronological Age:** If a building is well-maintained, its effective age is less than its chronological age. Always read the problem carefully. > 5. **Not stating units:** Always write "₹" or "Rs." or appropriate currency unit in the final answer. --- ### 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember - **Depreciation = Physical loss in value** due to wear, tear, age, and deterioration. - **Obsolescence = Non-physical loss in value** due to design flaws, outdated amenities, neighborhood decline, or locational shifts. - **Three types of obsolescence:** Functional, Economic (External), and Locational. - **Curable obsolescence** is economically feasible to fix; **incurable obsolescence** is not. - **Key formula:** $D.V. = RCN - (D_{physical} + O_{functional} + O_{economic})$ - **Straight-line depreciation formula:** $D = \frac{C \times (A - S)}{L}$ - **Capitalized obsolescence formula:** $O = \frac{L_{annual}}{R_c}$ - **Salvage value** is typically **10% of the original cost** unless specified. - **Effective age** may differ from chronological age based on maintenance quality. - **Always identify causes separately** before applying formulas in KTU numerical problems. - **Examiner's mantra:** "Physical = Depreciation; Design/External = Obsolescence." ---

topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PECET862 - VALUATION OF REAL PROPERTIES
> - **Module:** Module 3
> - **Topic:** Valuation for Bank: Purposes - Security, Primary and Collateral

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
# SECTION 1: CORE TECHNICAL DEFINITION & INTUITIVE OVERVIEW

## 1.1 Formal Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Terminology)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Valuation for Bank Purposes** is the specialized process of determining the **present market value**, **realizable value**, and **forced sale value** of a real property (land, building, or both) by a competent and approved valuer, for the purpose of providing an independent, unbiased, and technically sound opinion of the property's worth to a lending institution (bank or financial institution) against which a loan, mortgage, or financial accommodation is proposed to be sanctioned.

In the context of a bank's lending decision, the property offered by the borrower is broadly classified into two distinct categories of **Security**:

**A) Security (Umbrella Term):**
A comprehensive legal and financial term denoting the **entire bundle of assets** (both movable and immovable) that a borrower pledges, mortgages, hypothecates, or assigns to a bank as a safeguard against the recovery of the loan amount in the event of default.

**B) Primary Security:**
The asset that is **directly created, purchased, or financed** by the bank loan. It is the **principal and obvious asset** offered to the bank that is intrinsically connected with the end-use of the borrowed funds. The bank's first recourse in case of default is the primary security.

**C) Collateral Security:**
The **additional or supplementary asset(s)** offered by the borrower over and above the primary security, to **strengthen the bank's confidence** and to bridge any deficit in the value of the primary security relative to the loan amount. It acts as a **secondary line of defence** for the lender.

---

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Plain-English Intuition

> [!NOTE]
> **Real-World Analogy — The "House-Sitting and the Trusty Friend"**

Imagine you (the **borrower**) want to borrow ₹50 Lakhs from a friend (the **bank**) to buy a house. Your friend will not just hand over the money based on a verbal promise. He will ask: *"If you don't return the money, what do I get back?"*

1. **The house you are buying with that money** is the **PRIMARY SECURITY**. It is the *main thing* being bought with the loan, and it is the *first* thing the friend will claim if you default. *"If you don't pay, I take back the house I helped you buy."*

2. Now, suppose the house you wish to buy is old, located in a remote area, and your friend feels that the house alone is **not enough** to recover the full ₹50 Lakhs if you default. He then says: *"I am uncomfortable. Give me something EXTRA — perhaps your ancestral land, your FD receipts, or your gold jewellery."* This **extra item** is the **COLLATERAL SECURITY**. It is the *backup plan* — a safety net to make the friend feel doubly protected.

3. The **entire process** of your friend asking *"How much is this house actually worth in today's market?"* and getting a certified valuer to inspect and report the value is the **VALUATION FOR BANK PURPOSES**. The valuer tells the friend: *"This house is worth ₹60 Lakhs in the open market."* Now your friend feels safe to lend up to ₹48 Lakhs (keeping a **20% margin** of ₹12 Lakhs as his own safety cushion).

So:
- **Valuation** = The professional opinion of the property's worth.
- **Security** = The umbrella term for *everything* offered.
- **Primary** = The main asset (the house being bought).
- **Collateral** = The backup asset (the extra land/FD/gold).

---

## 1.3 Key Terminology & Standard Metrics (Highlighted)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Standard Banking Metrics to Memorise (Bold-emphasised):**

- **Market Value (MV):** The estimated amount for which a property would exchange on the date of valuation between a willing buyer and a willing seller in an arm's length transaction, after proper marketing. **Unit: ₹ (Rupees) or ₹ per sq.ft.**
- **Realizable Value:** The price a property would fetch if sold with **reasonable efforts within a reasonable time** (typically 85–90% of Market Value).
- **Forced Sale Value (FSV):** The price a property would fetch if sold **urgently under distressed conditions** (typically 70–80% of Market Value).
- **Margin (Haircut):** The percentage of the property value that the bank **does NOT finance**, kept as a cushion. **Standard: 20% to 30%** depending on property type and risk.
- **Loan-to-Value (LTV) Ratio:** The ratio of the loan amount sanctioned to the market value of the security. **Regulated by RBI: 75%–90%** depending on loan amount.
- **Security Coverage Ratio:** The ratio of the market value of all securities to the loan amount outstanding. Banks prefer **Security Coverage Ratio ≥ 1.25** (i.e., security value should be at least 125% of loan).
<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# SECTION 2: DEEP THEORETICAL ANALYSIS & KTU HIGH-YIELD FORMULA SHEET

## 2.1 The Logical Framework: Why Banks Need Valuation

Banks are **risk-averse financial intermediaries**. They accept deposits from the public (which carry an implicit guarantee of safety) and lend to borrowers (which carry an inherent credit risk). To balance this, banks follow the cardinal principle:

> [!IMPORTANT]
> *"Never lend more than what the security is worth, and always keep a margin."*

A bank's lending decision is governed by three pillars: **Creditworthiness of the Borrower (C), Capacity to Repay (C), and Collateral (C)** — the famous **"3 Cs of Credit"**. Valuation of real property directly supports the **Collateral (C)** pillar.

### The Step-by-Step Logic of Bank Valuation:

**Step 1 — Request for Loan:**
The borrower approaches the bank with a proposal (e.g., purchase a flat for ₹70 Lakhs, requests loan of ₹55 Lakhs).

**Step 2 — Identification of Security:**
The bank identifies what is being offered as security. Is it the flat being purchased? Is there additional land? Are there FDs? The bank classifies these into **Primary** and **Collateral**.

**Step 3 — Independent Valuation:**
The bank appoints an **approved/empaneled valuer** (an independent technical expert) to physically inspect the property, verify documents, and determine the **present market value** of the security.

**Step 4 — Application of Margin & LTV:**
The bank applies its internal **margin policy** (e.g., 25% for residential property). The **maximum loan amount** is then:
**Loan Amount = Market Value × (1 − Margin %)**
So: ₹70 Lakhs × 0.75 = **₹52.5 Lakhs** (which is LESS than the requested ₹55 Lakhs, so the bank caps the loan at ₹52.5 Lakhs).

**Step 5 — Sanction and Mortgage:**
The bank sanctions the loan amount, the property is **mortgaged** (legally transferred as security), and the loan is disbursed. The valuation report becomes a **permanent record** in the bank's loan file.

**Step 6 — Periodic Re-valuation (if required):**
For large loans, NPAs (Non-Performing Assets), or significant market shifts, the bank may order a **re-valuation** to ensure the security still adequately covers the outstanding loan.

---

## 2.2 Deep Dive: Primary Security vs. Collateral Security

The distinction between **Primary** and **Collateral** security is a high-frequency KTU examination topic. The following analytical matrix compares them across multiple dimensions:

| **Parameter** | **Primary Security** | **Collateral Security** |
|---|---|---|
| **Definition** | The main asset directly linked to the loan's end-use. | Additional asset(s) pledged to supplement the primary security. |
| **Purpose of Loan** | The loan is used to **acquire, construct, or improve** this asset. | The loan is **NOT used** for acquiring this asset. |
| **Legal Recourse** | The bank's **FIRST recourse** in case of default (SARFAESI Act, 2002). | The bank's **SECOND recourse** — invoked only if primary is insufficient. |
| **Examples** | House for a home loan; commercial building for a business loan; machinery for an equipment loan. | Ancestral land, additional flat, Fixed Deposits, LIC policies, gold, shares, third-party guarantee. |
| **Documentation** | Equitable Mortgage / Registered Mortgage / Hypothecation. | Equitable Mortgage / Pledge / Assignment / Lien. |
| **Valuation Focus** | Highest weightage — full technical valuation. | May need separate valuation or accepted at face value (e.g., FDs). |
| **Risk Weight (Banking)** | Lower risk weight (e.g., 50–75%). | Higher risk weight (e.g., 100–150%). |
| **Insurability** | Must be insured (comprehensively). | May or may not be insured. |
| **KTU Exam Phrasing** | "Main security" or "Principal security" | "Additional security" or "Subsidiary security" |

---

## 2.3 The Three "Faces" of Value in Bank Valuation

A KTU-savvy student must remember that a bank valuer is **not** asked to give only the **Market Value**. Banks specifically ask for **three values** to make prudent lending decisions:

1. **Market Value (MV)** — for loan eligibility calculation.
2. **Realizable Value (RV)** — for assessing the *practical* recovery amount in a reasonable timeframe. **RV ≈ 85% to 90% of MV**.
3. **Forced Sale Value (FSV)** — for the **worst-case scenario** (auction under SARFAESI). **FSV ≈ 70% to 80% of MV**.

> [!NOTE]
> **The Hierarchy of Values (from optimistic to pessimistic):**
> **Market Value ≥ Realizable Value ≥ Forced Sale Value**
> (MV > RV > FSV)

The bank will normally base its loan eligibility on **Market Value**, but will use the **FSV** to stress-test the security — i.e., *"Even if we are forced to auction the property under distressed conditions, will the FSV still cover the loan?"*

---

## 2.4 KTU Formula Sheet / High-Yield Cheat Sheet

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **The following formulas are the most frequently tested in KTU examinations for Module 3. Memorise the relationships, not just the symbols.**

| **#** | **Concept / Quantity** | **Formula** | **Explanation** | **Typical Unit / Value** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Loan Amount | $\text{Loan} = \text{MV} \times (1 - \text{Margin \%})$ | Bank finances only a portion of the Market Value. | ₹ (Rupees) |
| 2 | Loan-to-Value Ratio (LTV) | $\text{LTV} = \dfrac{\text{Loan Amount}}{\text{Market Value}} \times 100$ | Percentage of property value funded by the bank. | % (RBI: 75% – 90%) |
| 3 | Margin (Bank's Cushion) | $\text{Margin} = \text{MV} - \text{Loan Amount}$ | The bank's own risk buffer in absolute terms. | ₹ (Rupees) |
| 4 | Margin Percentage | $\text{Margin \%} = 100 - \text{LTV \%}$ | The unfinanced portion of the property value. | % (Typically 10% – 25%) |
| 5 | Security Coverage Ratio (SCR) | $\text{SCR} = \dfrac{\text{Total Market Value of Security}}{\text{Loan Amount}}$ | How many times the security covers the loan. | Ratio (≥ 1.25 preferred) |
| 6 | Realizable Value | $\text{RV} = \text{MV} \times \text{Realisation Factor}$ | Conservative market price after reasonable time. | ₹ (≈ 0.85 × MV to 0.90 × MV) |
| 7 | Forced Sale Value | $\text{FSV} = \text{MV} \times \text{FSV Factor}$ | Distress auction price. | ₹ (≈ 0.70 × MV to 0.80 × MV) |
| 8 | Distress Discount | $\text{Distress Discount} = \text{MV} - \text{FSV}$ | The cost of forced liquidation. | ₹ (Rupees) |
| 9 | Distress Discount % | $\text{Discount \%} = \dfrac{\text{MV} - \text{FSV}}{\text{MV}} \times 100$ | Stress-test cushion. | % (Typically 20% – 30%) |
| 10 | Combined Value (Multiple Securities) | $\text{Total Security} = \text{MV}_{\text{primary}} + \text{MV}_{\text{collateral}}$ | Aggregate value of all pledged assets. | ₹ (Rupees) |
| 11 | Effective LTV (with collateral) | $\text{Effective LTV} = \dfrac{\text{Loan}}{\text{MV}_{\text{primary}} + \text{MV}_{\text{collateral}}} \times 100$ | LTV after accounting for collateral support. | % |

---

## 2.5 Real-World Utility in Engineering & Banking Fields

- **Banking & Finance:** Foundation of mortgage underwriting, SARFAESI recovery, NPA resolution, and Basel-III capital adequacy norms.
- **Civil Engineering:** The valuer must understand structural soundness, age, depreciation, and remaining useful life of buildings — all civil engineering concepts directly applied.
- **Legal Profession:** Valuation reports are submitted as evidence in DRT (Debt Recovery Tribunal), SARFAESI courts, and consumer forums.
- **Insurance:** Banks insist on **comprehensive insurance** of the primary security (the property). The valuation determines the **sum insured**.
- **Public Sector:** Used by NHB (National Housing Bank), HUDCO, LIC Housing Finance, and state housing boards for bulk property finance.

# SECTION 3: STEP-BY-STEP DERIVATIONS & ANALYTICAL MATRIX

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Pedagogical Note:** The derivations below are deliberately written in exhaustive, granular steps because KTU board examiners reward **methodology** as much as final answers. Showing the logical progression of each formula from first principles ensures full marks.

---

## 3.1 Derivation: The Fundamental Loan-Value Equation

**Statement of the Problem (Axiom):**
A bank never finances the *entire* market value of a property. It deliberately keeps a portion (called **margin**) as its own risk capital. The bank's rule is:

> *"Maximum Loan = Market Value of Security minus a pre-defined Margin."*

### Step-by-Step Algebraic Derivation:

**Step 1:** Let the variables be defined as:
- $MV$ = Market Value of the property (₹)
- $L$ = Loan amount sanctioned by the bank (₹)
- $M$ = Margin kept by the bank in absolute terms (₹)
- $m$ = Margin expressed as a percentage (decimal form, e.g., 0.20 for 20%)

**Step 2:** The bank finances *whatever is left* after removing the margin. So, mathematically:
$$L = MV - M$$

**Step 3:** Now, the absolute margin $M$ is itself a *fraction* of the Market Value. By definition:
$$M = m \times MV$$

**Step 4:** Substitute Equation 3 into Equation 2:
$$L = MV - (m \times MV)$$

**Step 5:** Factor out the common term $MV$:
$$L = MV \times (1 - m)$$

**Step 6:** This is the **fundamental loan-amount equation**. The bank multiplies the market value by a **financing factor** $(1 - m)$ which is always less than 1.

**Step 7:** For example, if the bank policy is 25% margin (i.e., $m = 0.25$), the financing factor becomes $(1 - 0.25) = 0.75$. So the bank advances **75% of the market value** — the Loan-to-Value ratio is 75%.

---

## 3.2 Derivation: The Loan-to-Value (LTV) Ratio from First Principles

**Step 1:** By definition, LTV is the ratio of loan to property value, expressed as a percentage:
$$\text{LTV \%} = \frac{L}{MV} \times 100$$

**Step 2:** Substituting the expression for $L$ from Equation 5 of §3.1:
$$\text{LTV \%} = \frac{MV \times (1 - m)}{MV} \times 100$$

**Step 3:** The $MV$ terms cancel out (algebraic simplification):
$$\text{LTV \%} = (1 - m) \times 100$$

**Step 4:** Converting the decimal back to a percentage form, the **invariant relationship** is:
$$\text{LTV \%} + \text{Margin \%} = 100\%$$

**Step 5:** Worked example: If LTV is 80%, then Margin = 100% − 80% = 20%. If Margin is 30%, then LTV = 100% − 30% = 70%.

---

## 3.3 Derivation: Security Coverage Ratio (SCR)

**Step 1:** When there are *multiple* securities (primary + collateral), the total security is the sum of individual market values:
$$\text{Total Security} = MV_{\text{primary}} + MV_{\text{collateral}}$$

**Step 2:** The Security Coverage Ratio is defined as how many times the security "covers" the loan:
$$\text{SCR} = \frac{\text{Total Market Value of Security}}{\text{Loan Amount Outstanding}}$$

**Step 3:** For a bank to feel "safe," SCR should be at least 1.0 (security equals loan). For prudent lending, **SCR ≥ 1.25** (security is 125% of loan).

**Step 4:** Worked numerical example:
- Primary property MV = ₹60,00,000
- Collateral property MV = ₹20,00,000
- Loan sanctioned = ₹50,00,000
- Then: Total Security = ₹60,00,000 + ₹20,00,000 = ₹80,00,000
- SCR = ₹80,00,000 / ₹50,00,000 = **1.60** (Excellent coverage; the bank is well-protected).

---

## 3.4 Worked Numerical Problem: A KTU-Style Bank Valuation Calculation

> [!NOTE]
> **This is the exact type of 14-mark problem that appears in KTU End Semester Examinations. Solve it on your own, then verify against the model solution below.**

**Problem Statement:**
Mr. Ravi approaches a bank for a home loan of ₹80 Lakhs to purchase a residential flat. The bank's empaneled valuer submits the following report:
- Market Value of the flat (Primary Security) = **₹1,00,00,000**
- Market Value of an ancestral plot offered additionally (Collateral Security) = **₹30,00,000**
- Realisable Value of the flat = **₹90,00,000**
- Forced Sale Value of the flat = **₹75,00,000**

The bank's policy is:
- **Margin = 25%** on the Market Value of the flat.
- **LTV cap = 80%** of the total security value.

**Required:**
(a) Calculate the maximum loan amount the bank can sanction under both policies. Which policy is more restrictive? [7 Marks]
(b) Calculate the Security Coverage Ratio and comment on whether the security is adequate. If the flat had to be auctioned under SARFAESI, how much shortfall would the bank face assuming the entire loan is disbursed? [7 Marks]

---

### MODEL SOLUTION (with full step-by-step working):

### Part (a) Solution:

**Step 1 — Calculate Loan Eligibility under Margin Policy (25% on Flat MV):**

Using the fundamental loan equation from §3.1:
$$L_1 = MV_{\text{flat}} \times (1 - m)$$
$$L_1 = 1{,}00{,}00{,}000 \times (1 - 0.25)$$
$$L_1 = 1{,}00{,}00{,}000 \times 0.75$$
$$\boxed{L_1 = ₹75{,}00{,}000}$$

**Step 2 — Calculate Loan Eligibility under LTV Cap Policy (80% of Total Security):**

The LTV cap considers **both** primary and collateral securities:
$$L_2 = (MV_{\text{flat}} + MV_{\text{ancestral plot}}) \times \text{LTV \%}$$
$$L_2 = (1{,}00{,}00{,}000 + 30{,}00{,}000) \times 0.80$$
$$L_2 = 1{,}30{,}00{,}000 \times 0.80$$
$$\boxed{L_2 = ₹1{,}04{,}00{,}000}$$

**Step 3 — Identify the Restrictive Policy (the bank's golden rule):**

The bank will sanction the **LOWER** of the two amounts to protect itself:
$$L_{\text{sanctioned}} = \min(L_1, L_2) = \min(75{,}00{,}000, 1{,}04{,}00{,}000)$$
$$\boxed{L_{\text{sanctioned}} = ₹75{,}00{,}000}$$

**Conclusion of Part (a):** The **Margin Policy (25%)** is more restrictive. The bank will sanction **₹75 Lakhs**, which is **₹5 Lakhs less** than the borrower's request of ₹80 Lakhs. The borrower must arrange the balance ₹5 Lakhs from his own sources.

---

### Part (b) Solution:

**Step 1 — Calculate Security Coverage Ratio (SCR):**

Using the formula from §3.3:
$$\text{SCR} = \frac{MV_{\text{flat}} + MV_{\text{ancestral plot}}}{L_{\text{sanctioned}}}$$
$$\text{SCR} = \frac{1{,}00{,}00{,}000 + 30{,}00{,}000}{75{,}00{,}000}$$
$$\text{SCR} = \frac{1{,}30{,}00{,}000}{75{,}00{,}000}$$
$$\boxed{\text{SCR} = 1.733}$$

**Step 2 — Comment on Adequacy:**

Since the bank's prudent benchmark is **SCR ≥ 1.25**, the achieved SCR of **1.733** means the security is **highly adequate**. The bank is over-protected by approximately 73.3% above the loan amount.

**Step 3 — Calculate the Shortfall under Forced Sale (SARFAESI Auction):**

Under the **Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest (SARFAESI) Act, 2002**, the bank can auction the property under distressed conditions. In the worst case, both the primary and collateral may be sold at their forced sale values.

**Forced Sale Value of flat** = ₹75,00,000 (given in the report)
**Forced Sale Value of ancestral plot** = (Assuming typical 25% distress discount on collateral, since not given) = ₹30,00,000 × 0.75 = ₹22,50,000

**Total Recovery under FSV:**
$$\text{Total Recovery} = \text{FSV}_{\text{flat}} + \text{FSV}_{\text{ancestral plot}}$$
$$\text{Total Recovery} = 75{,}00{,}000 + 22{,}50{,}000 = ₹97{,}50{,}000$$

**Step 4 — Calculate Shortfall:**

$$\text{Shortfall} = L_{\text{sanctioned}} - \text{Total Recovery}$$
$$\text{Shortfall} = 75{,}00{,}000 - 97{,}50{,}000$$
$$\boxed{\text{Shortfall} = -₹22{,}50{,}000 \text{ (i.e., a SURPLUS, not a shortfall)}}$$

**Final Conclusion of Part (b):** Even under the **worst-case SARFAESI auction** scenario, the bank recovers **₹97.5 Lakhs** against a loan of **₹75 Lakhs** — a surplus of **₹22.5 Lakhs**. The security is **exceedingly adequate** and the borrower is in a very safe position. The bank should have no recovery concerns.

### Question A2: [KTU University Exam — Dec 2023, Model Question]
**"List the THREE values a bank valuer is required to estimate and write their relative hierarchy."**

**Model Answer (3 Marks):**

A bank-appointed valuer is required to estimate the following **three values** of the subject property:

1. **Market Value (MV):** The estimated price at which the property would sell in an open market between a willing buyer and willing seller on the date of valuation, with adequate marketing and no compulsion.

2. **Realisable Value (RV):** The price the property would fetch if sold with **reasonable efforts and within a reasonable timeframe** (typically **85% – 90% of Market Value**).

3. **Forced Sale Value (FSV):** The price the property would fetch in a **distress/auction sale** under legal compulsion such as SARFAESI proceedings (typically **70% – 80% of Market Value**).

**Hierarchy (from highest to lowest):**
$$\text{Market Value} \;>\; \text{Realisable Value} \;>\; \text{Forced Sale Value}$$

> [!IMPORTANT]
